templates.name: Main purpose: literary reaction, mood or trait
Function: example or supporting detail for a claim
Three moves: introduces a researcher, describes an aspect of the work, explains its significance
Function: qualification of an earlier description
Presents a philosophy or set of principles, then describes a work shaped by it
Presents the regard in which a character is held, then the behaviors that sustain it (literary prose)
Main purpose: profile of a person, work or institution
Introduces a person, then gives characteristics of their work

items.passage: Harbor seals are marine mammals, but a small population inhabits Alaska’s Iliamna Lake year-round. Because the lake is connected to the ocean by a 110-kilometer river, some researchers had hypothesized that seals regularly move between freshwater and marine habitats. Analyzing DNA extracted from seal scat and from tissue samples contributed by Indigenous hunters, Tatiana Ferrer and colleagues instead found the lake population to be genetically distinct from every marine population examined, including the nearest. Given the lake seals’ markedly reduced genetic diversity, a loss that would probably have required considerable time, the team concluded that the population has likely been isolated for an extended period.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It reports a surprising genetic pattern in a group of lake-dwelling animals and explains that the pattern shows the animals to be a different species from their relatives in the ocean.
It discusses a genetic study of a group of lake-dwelling animals in order to question whether samples contributed by hunters can reveal how those animals are related to others.
It presents an unexpected finding about a group of lake-dwelling animals and the reasoning behind researchers’ conclusion that the group has probably long been cut off from its relatives.
It presents an unexpected finding about a group of lake-dwelling animals and suggests that the group’s low genetic diversity indicates that it arrived in the lake from the ocean only recently.
items.explanation: Because the lake “is connected to the ocean by a 110-kilometer river,” some researchers expected seals to “regularly move between freshwater and marine habitats,” but Ferrer and colleagues “instead found the lake population to be genetically distinct from every marine population examined.” The text then gives the reasoning behind the team’s conclusion: the seals’ “markedly reduced genetic diversity” is “a loss that would probably have required considerable time,” so the population “has likely been isolated for an extended period.” Choice C names both the unexpected finding and that reasoning.

A.recipe: first clause true, later clause overreaches (BROAD)
A.why_wrong: The text does report a surprising genetic pattern, but it calls the lake seals “a small population” of harbor seals and never says they are a separate species. Its conclusion concerns how long the population “has likely been isolated,” not what species it belongs to.

B.why_wrong: The samples “contributed by Indigenous hunters” are simply part of the evidence the team analyzed. The text never questions what they can reveal; it reports what the DNA showed and what the team concluded from it.

D.recipe: first clause true, later clause reversed (REV)
D.why_wrong: The finding is unexpected, but the text draws the opposite conclusion from the low diversity: losing it “would probably have required considerable time,” so the population “has likely been isolated for an extended period” rather than having arrived recently.

sources.what: Ferrer, Boveng, Hauser, Withrow, Burkanov, Quinn and O’Corry-Crowe 2024, Biology Letters 20: 20240166 (PMC full text; PubMed 39406337): about 400 harbour seals live year-round in Iliamna Lake, Alaska, which drains to Bristol Bay through the 110 km Kvichak River, so seals could move between the two; earlier hypotheses that dispersal regularly occurs between the lake and marine habitats; DNA from seal scat and tissue samples provided by Indigenous hunters; the lake seals are genetically discrete from all eight Pacific regions sampled, including the nearest (Bristol Bay), with less genetic diversity and more inbreeding; losing that diversity would likely have required a substantial amount of time; the lake seals have likely been isolated long enough for marked divergence (“striking and unexpected”)

items.notes: Area: natural science (population genetics). Key C. Written in review to replace a stick-insect draft (Ramulus mikado, eggs surviving a bird’s gut) judged a concept twin of live boundaries.S2_colon.hard.w1b1_06 (Japanese snails surviving passage through white-eyes and bulbuls). Key parts: 2 (an unexpected finding; the reasoning behind a hedged conclusion). Section 6 checks: key 29 words; options 29 to 31 words; all three distractors keep a true first clause and fail later (A an invented species claim, B a wrong purpose for the right study, D a reversed reading of the low diversity). The premise is the genetic isolation of a lake population, not the route by which seals reached a lake (live boundaries.S6_question.easy.w3b2_21, Baikal seal). Register is held near CB’s hard figure because the tier also carries a literary excerpt.
band7_moves: dual, hedged purpose as in 82cb7dda: the key joins the finding with the reasoning behind a hedged conclusion (“probably long been cut off”)
abstract key: “a group of lake-dwelling animals” and “cut off from its relatives” replace seals, Iliamna, DNA and marine populations
three-option first-clause match: A, B and D open with a true account (a surprising pattern, a genetic study, an unexpected finding) and fail on a later link

fixes: replaced the subject: the stick-insect draft (Ramulus mikado eggs surviving a bird’s gut, Suetsugu et al. 2023) was a concept twin of live boundaries.S2_colon.hard.w1b1_06 (Japanese snails surviving passage through white-eyes and bulbuls); rewritten on Iliamna Lake harbor seals (Ferrer et al. 2024, PMC full text fetched), same key letter and option shapes; new subject grepped and claimed, stick-insect claim withdrawn in claims.txt
register held near CB’s hard figure (hard tier 5.24 chars per word, floor 5.23) because the tier carries a literary excerpt
re-solved blind after the rewrite: C

band7.why: dual, hedged purpose as in 82cb7dda; abstract key with no passage nouns; all three distractors keep a true first clause and fail on a later link, and D (low diversity means a recent arrival) is the familiar reading that the passage’s appositive reverses; one defensible answer

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Charles Lamb’s 1825 essay “The Superannuated Man.” The narrator has just retired after more than thirty years as a clerk.

For the first day or two I felt stunned, overwhelmed. I could only apprehend my felicity; I was too confused to taste it sincerely. I wandered about, thinking I was happy, and knowing that I was not. I could scarce trust myself with myself. From a poor man, poor in Time, I was suddenly lifted up into a vast revenue; I could see no end of my possessions; I wanted some steward, or judicious bailiff, to manage my estates in Time for me.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It conveys the narrator’s initial difficulty in enjoying a change of circumstances that he regards as fortunate.
It reveals the narrator’s growing suspicion that a change he had long hoped for has left him worse off than before.
It describes the narrator’s uncertainty about how to invest the money that he saved during his many years of work.
It presents the narrator’s attempt to convince himself that a change he had long dreaded has in fact turned out well.
items.explanation: The narrator calls his retirement “my felicity” and says he has been “lifted up into a vast revenue” of time, so he regards the change as fortunate. Yet “for the first day or two” he was “too confused to taste it sincerely,” wandering about “thinking I was happy, and knowing that I was not.” The text therefore conveys his early difficulty in enjoying a change he considers lucky, as choice A says.

B.why_wrong: The narrator is not yet happy, but he never suggests he is worse off. He calls the change “my felicity” and speaks of “a vast revenue,” and his confusion is limited to “the first day or two,” not a growing suspicion.

C.why_wrong: The “revenue,” “possessions,” and “estates” are figurative: he was “poor in Time” and is now rich in it, wanting a steward “to manage my estates in Time.” The text says nothing about money he saved.

D.why_wrong: The line “thinking I was happy, and knowing that I was not” describes confusion, not an effort at self-persuasion, and nothing in the text suggests he had dreaded retiring; he calls it “my felicity.”

sources.what: Charles Lamb, “The Superannuated Man” (London Magazine, May 1825; Last Essays of Elia), in The Works of Charles and Mary Lamb, vol. 2, Project Gutenberg 10343: sentences 1 to 3, 5 and 8 of the paragraph after “Esto perpetua!”, copied exactly (the Bastille sentence and two sentences on Time and Eternity left out); the essay says the narrator took his seat at the desk “six and thirty years” before

items.notes: Literature (essay, 1825). Key A. Key parts: 2 (the change is fortunate; he cannot enjoy it at first). Section 6 checks: key 20 words; options 18 to 20 words; B keeps a true first part (he is not happy) and reverses the judgment; C literalizes the time-as-wealth figure; D misreads the “thinking I was happy” line. Short, abstract key with no passage nouns, as in b0f7541b.
band7_moves: archaic prose (1825) whose point is carried by a paradox the student must resolve: happiness he “knows” he does not feel, and wealth that is only time
abstract key (“a change of circumstances that he regards as fortunate”) with no passage nouns
near-miss distractors: B keeps the unease and reverses the verdict; C turns the extended money figure literal; D misreads the key line as self-persuasion

fixes: excerpt checked against Gutenberg 10343 (five sentences exact, three left out as noted); context line confirmed (“six and thirty years”)

C rewritten from “how to manage the wealth that his many years of work have brought him” to money he saved: read figuratively (his wealth of Time came from retiring after years of work), the old C came close to defensible; why_wrong C updated

band7.why: archaic 1825 prose whose point rests on two paradoxes (happiness he knows he does not feel, wealth that is only time); short abstract key as in b0f7541b; B keeps the unease and reverses the verdict, C literalizes the money figure, D misreads the “thinking I was happy” line

items.passage: In the 1930s, the Irish Folklore Commission was charged with documenting the oral traditions of Ireland, but its limited budget typically allowed it to employ only six to nine collectors. Between 1937 and 1939, the commission found a way around that constraint in the nation’s classrooms: teachers at primary schools throughout what is now the Republic of Ireland assigned a topic each week, and their pupils—<u>more than 50,000 children in all</u>—interviewed parents, grandparents, and neighbors and transcribed their recollections. The resulting Schools’ Collection comprises more than 375,000 handwritten pages.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It underscores how many children took part in the project in order to explain why some teachers objected to devoting class time to it.
It indicates how many children took part in the project, a figure that the text suggests made their accounts less reliable than those of trained collectors.
It gives the number of children involved in the project to help explain the limit on the commission’s budget that is mentioned earlier in the text.
It underscores the scale of the participation that enabled the commission to overcome the limitation on its work described earlier in the text.
items.explanation: The first sentence says the commission’s “limited budget typically allowed it to employ only six to nine collectors.” The next says the commission “found a way around that constraint in the nation’s classrooms,” and the underlined portion gives the number of pupils who did the collecting: “more than 50,000 children in all.” Set against six to nine collectors, the figure underscores the scale of the participation that enabled the commission to overcome its limit, as choice D says.

A.recipe: first clause true, later clause invents a controversy (INV)
A.why_wrong: The figure does show how many children took part, but the text never mentions teachers objecting; it says only that teachers “assigned a topic each week.”

B.recipe: first clause true, later clause invents a judgment (INV)
B.why_wrong: The portion does give the number of children, but the text never questions the reliability of their accounts or compares them with those of trained collectors.

C.recipe: first clause true, wrong relation to the earlier sentence (REL)
C.why_wrong: The figure does not explain the budget limit. The first sentence gives that limit as the reason the commission could employ “only six to nine collectors,” and the children were the commission’s “way around that constraint.”

sources.what: Wikipedia, Irish Folklore Commission: with funding at a limit the commission was often limited to six to nine collectors; the Schools’ Collection (1937 to 1939) was written by more than 50,000 schoolchildren from all primary schools in the south of Ireland, the teacher choosing a heading each week and the children questioning family members and neighbors; 375,660 pages by June 1939

items.notes: Area: history (folklore collecting). Key D. Key parts: 2 (the scale of participation; how it overcame the limit stated earlier). Section 6 checks: key 24 words; options 23 to 26 words; distractors with a true first clause and a false later clause: A, B and C (3 of 3, as in 1f2d6173). The deciding clue sits in the sentence before the span (six to nine collectors). Review: C now points back to the earlier sentence with the wrong relation, as the key does, so the key is no longer the only option that looks back.
band7_moves: number span whose job is to show extent, as in 2e744883 (“more than 7,000 in all”)
the key needs a sentence outside the span: the figure matters only against the “six to nine collectors” of the first sentence
A and B open with a true account of the figure and invent a later clause (an objection, a reliability judgment)

fixes: core claim confirmed (Wikipedia, Irish Folklore Commission: six to nine collectors, 1937 to 1939, more than 50,000 schoolchildren, 375,660 pages)
C rewritten as a wrong relation to the first sentence (REL), so D is no longer the only option that refers back to earlier text

band7.why: number span that shows extent, as in 2e744883 (“more than 7,000 in all”); the key needs the first sentence’s “six to nine collectors”; all three distractors give the figure correctly and fail later, and C now also points back to the first sentence with the wrong relation, so looking back no longer singles out the key

items.passage: Soon after the metronome was patented in 1815, Beethoven added tempo markings to his eight published symphonies, and musicians have disputed them ever since: many consider the indicated tempos too fast to be performed well, while others insist that the markings express the composer’s wishes. Some have even blamed a faulty metronome. But analyzing 36 recorded performances by different conductors, Almudena Martín-Castro and Iñaki Ucar found that the performances ran slower than marked by a strikingly consistent margin—one that could result from reading the metronome’s scale below its sliding weight rather than above it.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To argue that conductors should finally adopt the tempos a composer marked, since research has shown that his metronome worked properly
To present research indicating that a long-standing disagreement over a composer’s instructions may stem from a simple misreading
To describe research showing that a faulty metronome led a composer to mark tempos considerably faster than he had intended
To explain why conductors in recent decades have chosen slower tempos for a composer’s symphonies than earlier conductors did
items.explanation: The text first describes a dispute: “many consider the indicated tempos too fast,” while “others insist that the markings express the composer’s wishes.” It then reports that Martín-Castro and Ucar found performances slower “by a strikingly consistent margin,” one that “could result from reading the metronome’s scale below its sliding weight rather than above it.” The text thus presents research suggesting that the dispute may come from a misreading, as choice B says.

A.why_wrong: The text does turn away from the “faulty metronome” explanation, but it never urges conductors to do anything. If anything, the finding suggests the markings are too fast because of a misreading, not that they should be followed.

C.why_wrong: The faulty metronome is the view the text sets aside (“Some have even blamed a faulty metronome. But...”). The researchers’ margin “could result from reading the metronome’s scale” wrongly, not from a defect in the device.

D.why_wrong: The study compares performances with Beethoven’s markings, not conductors of one period with those of another. The text never says tempos have changed over time.

sources.what: Martín-Castro and Ucar 2020, PLOS ONE (PubMed abstract; PMC7743971 full text): Beethoven added metronome marks to his eight published symphonies after Maelzel’s 1815 patent; many musicians consider them too quick, others claim them as his will; tempos extracted from 36 recordings by different conductors show a systematic deviation (always slower on average, about 12 bpm); the model of Maelzel’s metronome rules out the broken-metronome hypothesis; the hasty marks could be explained by reading the scale below the weight instead of above

items.notes: Area: humanities (music history). Key B. Band 6 (P_view has one band-7 official, but this cell is planned band 6). Key parts: 2 (a long dispute; a study tracing it to a possible misreading). Wrong options each keep a true element: A the turn away from a faulty device, C the topic of markings that run fast, D the conductors’ tempos. The passage hedges the cause as the source does (“could be explained,” “matches the error”).

fixes: core claim confirmed (PubMed 33326433)
hedged as the source does: “one that matches the error that would result from reading” to “one that could result from reading” (abstract: “could be explained by”); explanation and why_wrong C updated
fame call: kept; Beethoven is famous, but the 2020 scale-misreading finding is not class knowledge and the key needs it; Beethoven appears in two CB CID items only in passing

band7.why: planned band 6; a strong P_view: the key needs the turn and the hedged misreading, C adopts the faulty-metronome view the text sets aside, A and D keep true elements; each wrong option still fails on one stated point, so not band 7

items.passage: Hugh Tracey, a British-born ethnomusicologist, became fascinated by African music in the 1920s while working on a tobacco farm in what is now Zimbabwe. Over the following five decades he made more than 35,000 field recordings throughout southern and central Africa, deliberately seeking out rural communities whose traditional music, he feared, was disappearing under the pressures of modern life. The International Library of African Music, which he founded in 1954 and which preserves his recordings, is today the largest repository of Indigenous African music.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It introduces a researcher, describes the purpose behind the extensive work he undertook, and notes the present-day standing of the archive that houses that work.
It introduces a researcher, describes the purpose behind his extensive work, and then explains why later scholars have questioned whether his recordings capture traditional music.
It describes the decline of a region’s traditional music, explains which modern influences were responsible for it, and presents a researcher’s plan to revive that music.
It introduces a researcher, explains how he came to play the instruments he later recorded, and describes the farm on which he first heard them played.
items.explanation: The first sentence introduces Hugh Tracey and how he “became fascinated by African music.” The second describes his “more than 35,000 field recordings” and the purpose behind them: he sought out communities “whose traditional music, he feared, was disappearing under the pressures of modern life.” The third notes that the library preserving the recordings “is today the largest repository of Indigenous African music.” Choice A follows these three moves.

B.recipe: moves 1 and 2 right, move 3 stance invented (STANCE)
B.why_wrong: The first two moves fit, but the text never mentions later scholars or doubts about the recordings; it ends by noting that the library is “the largest repository of Indigenous African music.”

C.why_wrong: The text mentions only Tracey’s fear that music “was disappearing under the pressures of modern life.” It names no particular influences and describes no plan to revive anything; Tracey recorded the music.

D.why_wrong: The text introduces Tracey, but it never says he learned to play any instrument, and the tobacco farm is mentioned only in passing as where he worked when his interest began.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Hugh Tracey: British ethnomusicologist; became interested in local music while farming tobacco in Southern Rhodesia (now Zimbabwe) in the late 1920s; made over 35,000 recordings in Southern and Central Africa from the 1920s to the 1970s; wanted to stop the loss of traditional music to modernity and recorded in rural areas; founded the International Library of African Music in 1954 (the ILAM article calls it the largest repository of indigenous African music)

items.notes: Area: humanities (ethnomusicology). Key A. Band 6: S13 has no band-7 official item (spec/rw/band7/text_structure_and_purpose.md), so written as a strong band 6. Three moves; B and D keep the first one or two moves and break the last, as hard S distractors do (3.6, 3.17). Second source for the archive claim: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Library_of_African_Music.

fixes: core claim confirmed (Wikipedia, Hugh Tracey and International Library of African Music); subject is distinct from the live Maceda and early-phonograph field-recording items

band7.why: S13 has no band-7 official item (spec/rw/band7/text_structure_and_purpose.md), so it cannot be band 7; a strong band 6 in which B keeps moves 1 and 2 and breaks move 3, as hard S distractors do

items.passage:
The following text is from Abraham Cahan’s 1896 novel Yekl: A Tale of the New York Ghetto. Jake, who emigrated from Russia to New York three years earlier, has come to Ellis Island to meet his wife, Gitl, and their young son, Yosselé, who have just arrived.

All the way to the island he had been in a flurry of joyous anticipation. The prospect of meeting his dear wife and child, and, incidentally, of showing off his swell attire to her, had thrown him into a fever of impatience. But on entering the big shed he had caught a distant glimpse of Gitl and Yosselé through the railing separating the detained immigrants from their visitors, and his heart had sunk at the sight of his wife’s uncouth and un-American appearance.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To show that a character regrets having left his family behind when he moved to another country
To describe the difficulties that newly arrived immigrants faced while being held at Ellis Island
To explain why a character has chosen to wear his finest clothes to meet his wife and child
To portray how a character’s eager anticipation of a reunion gives way to dismay
items.explanation: On the way to the island Jake “had been in a flurry of joyous anticipation” and “a fever of impatience” to meet his wife and child. But when he glimpsed Gitl, “his heart had sunk at the sight of his wife’s uncouth and un-American appearance.” The text traces this shift from eagerness to dismay, as choice D says.

A.why_wrong: Jake’s feelings concern meeting Gitl, not having left her; his “heart had sunk” at her appearance, which is not regret about leaving his family.

B.why_wrong: The text mentions “the detained immigrants” only to say where Jake glimpsed Gitl. It describes Jake’s feelings, not what immigrants went through.

C.recipe: one detail taken for the whole (PART)
C.why_wrong: The text mentions “showing off his swell attire” only as part of Jake’s excitement on the way; the excerpt turns on how that excitement collapses when he sees Gitl.

sources.what: Abraham Cahan, Yekl: A Tale of the New York Ghetto (1896), chapter “A Defeat,” Project Gutenberg 36715: the second paragraph of the Ellis Island scene, copied exactly (three sentences, to “un-American appearance”); Jake has sent for Gitl and Yosselé from Russia

items.notes: Literature (novel, 1896). Key D. Distractors: A invents a regret, B hooks on “detained immigrants” and widens the scope, C takes one detail (the clothes) for the purpose. Key is the shortest option, as in 2.7 and 1.5.

fixes: excerpt checked against Gutenberg 36715 (contiguous, exact)
context line: “several years earlier” to “three years earlier” (Cahan: “some three years before the opening of this story”)

items.passage:
The following text is from Amelia Opie’s 1804 novel Adeline Mowbray. Mrs Mowbray, Adeline’s mother, is admired for her learning and devotes most of her time to study. When Adeline was a girl, Mrs Mowbray nursed her through a dangerous illness.

Not even the parents of Mrs Mowbray, who, because she talked on subjects which they could not understand, looked up to her as a superior being, could exceed Adeline in deference to her mother’s abilities; and when, as she advanced in life, she was sometimes tempted to think her deficient in maternal fondness, the idea of Mrs Mowbray bending with pale and speechless anxiety over her sleepless pillow used to recur to her remembrance, and in a moment the recent indifference was forgotten.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To suggest that Adeline’s grandparents admire Mrs Mowbray’s learning far more than Adeline does
To convey how the memory of a past kindness keeps a character’s doubts about her mother’s affection from lasting
To explain why Mrs Mowbray, once devoted to her daughter, grew less attentive after the girl recovered from her illness
To portray Adeline’s gradual discovery that her mother’s abilities are less impressive than others believe
items.explanation: Adeline is “sometimes tempted to think” her mother “deficient in maternal fondness.” But whenever that happens, “the idea of Mrs Mowbray bending with pale and speechless anxiety over her sleepless pillow” returns to her, “and in a moment the recent indifference was forgotten.” The memory of her mother’s care during the illness ends Adeline’s doubts each time, as choice B says.

A.why_wrong: The text says the opposite: “Not even the parents of Mrs Mowbray” could “exceed Adeline in deference to her mother’s abilities.”

C.why_wrong: The text mentions Mrs Mowbray’s “recent indifference” only as Adeline sometimes perceives it; it never explains it or ties it to the end of the illness.

D.why_wrong: Adeline’s “deference to her mother’s abilities” is as great as anyone’s; her doubts concern her mother’s fondness, not her abilities.

sources.what: Amelia Opie, Adeline Mowbray; or, The Mother and Daughter (1804), chapter II, Project Gutenberg 37908: the paragraph beginning “Not even the parents of Mrs Mowbray,” copied exactly (one sentence); the preceding paragraph tells of Adeline’s twenty-one-day illness and her mother’s nursing, and the chapter describes Mrs Mowbray’s absorption in study

items.notes: Literature (novel, 1804). Key B. Distractors: A reverses the comparison with the grandparents, C invents a cause, D shifts the doubt from fondness to abilities. One long periodic sentence, as in older medium excerpts (2.6).

fixes: excerpt checked against Gutenberg 37908 (one sentence, exact); context confirmed (the twenty-one-day illness and her mother’s nursing)

items.passage: Owls combine sharp vision in dim light with acute hearing to hunt in darkness, but such sensory adaptations were long unknown among nonavian dinosaurs. <u>Examining features of the eyes and inner ears of living and extinct species, Jonah Choiniere and colleagues found that Shuvuuia deserti, a small Late Cretaceous dinosaur from Mongolia, had vision suited to extremely low light and hearing that rivaled the barn owl’s.</u> The researchers concluded that Shuvuuia probably hunted at night, and that this combination of abilities arose in dinosaurs long before modern birds appeared.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It explains why the sensory adaptations mentioned in the previous sentence were difficult to identify in dinosaurs.
It describes a method of studying fossils that the following sentence suggests produced unreliable results.
It presents findings that support the conclusion about Shuvuuia’s behavior stated in the following sentence.
It introduces a comparison between owls and dinosaurs that the following sentence shows to be mistaken.
items.explanation: The underlined sentence reports what Choiniere and colleagues found: Shuvuuia “had vision suited to extremely low light and hearing that rivaled the barn owl’s.” The next sentence draws the conclusion these traits support: “Shuvuuia probably hunted at night.” So the underlined sentence presents findings that support the conclusion in the following sentence, as choice C says.

A.why_wrong: The first sentence says only that the adaptations “were long unknown”; the underlined sentence reports a finding and does not explain why they were hard to identify.

B.why_wrong: The following sentence builds on the method’s results (“The researchers concluded...”); nothing in it suggests they were unreliable.

D.recipe: reversed relation to the next sentence (REV)
D.why_wrong: The comparison with the barn owl is not overturned: the following sentence concludes that Shuvuuia, like owls, “probably hunted at night.”

sources.what: Choiniere et al. 2021, Science (PubMed abstract): owls and nightbirds combine visual and hearing adaptations for nocturnal hunting; such sensory innovations were unknown in nonavialan theropods; proxies of vision and hearing in living and extinct theropods; nocturnal predation evolved early in Alvarezsauroidea (extreme low-light vision, increased hearing sensitivity); the Late Cretaceous alvarezsauroid Shuvuuia deserti had hearing acuity rivaling the barn owl’s; the combination evolved in dinosaurs long before the modern bird radiation
Wikipedia, Shuvuuia: a bird-like theropod from the Late Cretaceous of Mongolia, known from Ukhaa Tolgod and Tögrögiin Shiree in the Djadochta Formation

items.notes: Area: natural science (paleontology). Key C. Function family: supporting detail for a claim in the following sentence (2.1). Distractors: A a REL label (explains why), B a stance flip on the next sentence, D a reversed link. Shuvuuia is from the Djadochta Formation of Mongolia (second source, checked in review; not the item’s premise).

fixes: core claim confirmed (PubMed 33958472)
“Mongolia” confirmed (Wikipedia, Shuvuuia: Djadochta Formation, Mongolia), added as a second source and the note corrected

items.passage: In many low-income countries, tuberculosis is diagnosed mainly by looking at patients’ sputum under a microscope, a test that misses many infections. Alan Poling and colleagues have reported results from a supplementary form of screening. <u>African giant pouched rats, trained to recognize the odor of the disease, sniff sputum samples that have already been examined under the microscope and signal those that smell of tuberculosis.</u> In 2014, this screening found 1,412 more patients in Tanzania and 645 in Mozambique, increases of 39 percent and 53 percent over microscopy alone.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It describes how the supplementary screening discussed in the text is carried out.
It explains how the rats used in the screening were selected and bred.
It presents a hypothesis about tuberculosis that the following sentence casts doubt on.
It explains why microscopes often fail to detect tuberculosis in sputum samples.
items.explanation: The second sentence says Poling and colleagues “have reported results from a supplementary form of screening.” The underlined sentence explains how that screening works: trained rats “sniff sputum samples that have already been examined under the microscope and signal those that smell of tuberculosis.” The last sentence then gives its results. So the underlined sentence describes how the screening is carried out, as choice A says.

B.why_wrong: The sentence says the rats are “trained to recognize the odor of the disease,” but it says nothing about how they were chosen or bred.

C.why_wrong: The underlined sentence describes a procedure, not a hypothesis, and the following sentence reports the procedure’s success rather than casting doubt on anything.

D.why_wrong: The first sentence says microscopy is “a test that misses many infections,” but no sentence explains why, and the underlined sentence is about the rats.

sources.what: Poling et al. 2017, Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis (PubMed abstract): TB is a major problem in poor countries because sensitive diagnostic tools are unavailable; in 2014 pouched rats evaluated sputum from 21,600 Tanzanians and 9,048 Mozambicans previously evaluated by microscopy, the standard diagnostic; the rats revealed 1,412 new patients in Tanzania and 645 in Mozambique, increases of 39% and 53% over microscopy alone

items.notes: Area: natural science (public health, animal detection). Key A. Function: method (2.20, “describe an approach”). Distractors: B invents a detail of the method, C a REL label with a wrong pointer, D the first sentence’s topic plus an invented cause. The source does not detail how rats signal; the passage says only that they “signal.”

fixes: core claim confirmed (PubMed 27718224)

items.passage: <u>In polyembryony, a single fertilized egg divides repeatedly to produce several genetically identical embryos.</u> The parasitic wasp Copidosoma floridanum carries this process to an extreme: a female lays her eggs inside the egg of a moth, and as the moth caterpillar grows, each wasp egg multiplies into a brood of hundreds or even thousands of clones. Some of these larvae become sterile soldiers that never mature. In a 2019 study, Takuya Otsuki and colleagues reported that female soldiers kill most of the male larvae sharing their host, a mass killing that, by the researchers’ calculations, ultimately benefits the males’ own genes.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the first sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It identifies a problem that researchers studying parasitic wasps have been unable to solve.
It presents a claim about insect reproduction that the 2019 study calls into question.
It describes a hypothesis that is tested in the following sentence using data from moths.
It defines a process that the rest of the text illustrates with an unusual case.
items.explanation: The first sentence explains what polyembryony is: “a single fertilized egg divides repeatedly to produce several genetically identical embryos.” The next sentence says Copidosoma floridanum “carries this process to an extreme,” and the rest of the text describes that wasp’s broods and soldier larvae. So the first sentence defines a process that the text goes on to illustrate, as choice D says.

A.why_wrong: The first sentence describes how polyembryony works; it does not present it as a problem, and the text mentions nothing researchers have failed to solve.

B.why_wrong: The 2019 study concerns female soldiers killing male larvae; it does not question the definition of polyembryony, which the wasp’s broods exemplify.

C.why_wrong: The first sentence states a definition, not a hypothesis, and the moth appears only as the host in which the wasp lays its eggs.

fixes: core claim confirmed (PubMed 31089143; Wikipedia, Copidosoma floridanum)

The following text is from Charles Reade’s 1853 novel Peg Woffington. Sir Charles Pomander has been led to believe that Mrs. Vane, a young wife he hopes to court, is waiting for him alone in Triplet’s house. The woman waiting for him is in fact the actress Peg Woffington, wearing Mrs. Vane’s hood.

He found in Triplet’s house a lady who seemed startled at her late hardihood [boldness]. She sat with her back to the door, her hood drawn tightly down, and wore an air of trembling consciousness. Sir Charles smiled again. He knew the sex [women], <u>at least he said so</u>. (It is an assertion often ventured upon.) Accordingly Sir Charles determined to come down from his height, and court nature and innocence in their own tones.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined phrase in the text as a whole?
options: It reveals that Sir Charles himself doubts that he will succeed in charming Mrs. Vane.
It qualifies a claim about Sir Charles’s understanding of women.
It emphasizes how nervous the woman in Triplet’s house appears to be.
It suggests that Sir Charles has seen through the woman’s disguise.
items.explanation: The narrator first states that Sir Charles “knew the sex,” then adds “at least he said so,” turning the statement into a mere claim of Sir Charles’s own. The parenthesis that follows, “It is an assertion often ventured upon,” confirms the doubt. The underlined phrase therefore qualifies the claim about Sir Charles’s understanding of women, as choice B says.

A.recipe: doubt given to the wrong person (SWAP)
A.why_wrong: The doubt belongs to the narrator, not to Sir Charles, who “smiled again” and confidently decides how to court the woman.

C.why_wrong: The woman’s nervousness, her “air of trembling consciousness,” is described in an earlier sentence; the underlined phrase concerns Sir Charles.

D.why_wrong: Sir Charles is fooled: he plans to court “nature and innocence,” the manner suited to Mrs. Vane, not to an actress in disguise.

items.passage: Landscape architect Kongjian Yu argued that cities should behave like sponges: instead of relying only on pipes and concrete channels to rush rainwater away, they should use wetlands, parks, and other green spaces to absorb it, store it, and release it gradually. Qunli Stormwater Park, designed by Yu’s firm for a rapidly developing district of Harbin, China, puts that idea into practice. Around a protected wetland that new roads and buildings had cut off from its water sources, the designers dug a ring of ponds and raised mounds that collect, cleanse, and store the district’s stormwater.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

It presents an approach to managing rainwater and then explains why that approach failed in one city.
It presents a principle for handling rainwater in cities and then describes a project designed according to that principle.
It describes a wetland threatened by development and then argues that the city should have protected it by law.
items.explanation: The first sentence presents Yu’s principle that cities “should behave like sponges,” using green spaces “to absorb it, store it, and release it gradually.” The rest of the text describes Qunli Stormwater Park, which “puts that idea into practice” with ponds and mounds that “collect, cleanse, and store the district’s stormwater.” Choice C describes this structure.

A.why_wrong: Only one landscape architect, Yu, is named, and the text reports no disagreement.

B.why_wrong: The text presents the sponge approach, but it says the park “puts that idea into practice”; it reports no failure.

D.recipe: detail taken as the first move, invented argument (STANCE)
D.why_wrong: The wetland is already “protected,” and the text describes how the park was built around it; it never argues for any law.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Samuel Butler’s 1903 novel The Way of All Flesh. Theobald Pontifex is the clergyman of Battersby, a country parish.

Who so integer vitæ scelerisque purus [blameless], it was asked, as Mr Pontifex of Battersby? Who so fit to be consulted if any difficulty about parish management should arise? Who such a happy mixture of the sincere uninquiring Christian and of the man of the world? For so people actually called him. They said he was such an admirable man of business. His constitutional timidity rendered him incapable of an attempt to overreach [cheat] when there was the remotest chance of opposition or publicity, and his correct bearing and somewhat stern expression were a great protection to him against being overreached.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It reports the high opinion that the people around Theobald hold of him and then identifies traits of his that help account for that opinion.
It reports the high opinion that the people around Theobald hold of him and then recounts the business dealings that first earned him that opinion.
It describes the suspicion with which Theobald is regarded in Battersby and then explains the steps he takes to overcome it.
It contrasts Theobald’s reputation in his parish with his reputation in his own family and then suggests which of the two is more accurate.
items.explanation: The first five sentences give what people say of Theobald: no one is so blameless or so “fit to be consulted,” he is “such a happy mixture” of Christian and man of the world, “such an admirable man of business.” The last sentence names traits behind that view: his “constitutional timidity” keeps him from cheating, and “his correct bearing and somewhat stern expression” keep others from cheating him. Choice A describes this structure.

B.why_wrong: People call him “an admirable man of business,” but the text recounts no business dealings; it names his timidity, bearing, and expression.

C.why_wrong: Theobald is admired, not suspected: “Who so integer vitæ scelerisque purus [blameless], it was asked, as Mr Pontifex of Battersby?”

D.why_wrong: The text gives only the opinion of the people around him; his family is never mentioned.

The following text is adapted from Edward Bok’s 1920 autobiography The Americanization of Edward Bok, which Bok wrote in the third person. Edward, a boy whose family has recently immigrated from the Netherlands, is standing outside a bakery near his home.

The owner of the bakery, who had just placed in the window a series of trays filled with buns, tarts, and pies, came outside to look at the display. items.passage: Birds and mammals keep their bodies warm by producing heat internally. <u>This capacity is known as “endothermy.”</u> Most reptiles lack it and depend instead on outside sources of heat, such as sunlight.
